sources.title: SANTS: A State-Adaptive Scheduler for World Action Models

3.2 Stopping Hazard and Relative Noise Progression
C Reinforcement-Learning Post-Training and Reward Definition

tablesReviewed: Table 3: success-rate cells; Full WAM and SANTS latency checked against accompanying prose

synopsis: SANTS learns how much future-video denoising a robot policy needs before generating an action chunk. A small scheduler controls both stopping and the next noise level while the video–action policy remains frozen. Its reward measures demonstrated-action agreement and computation, rather than video appearance. The experiments support a better success–latency tradeoff than full denoising, although faster external policies remain available. The supplied title, identifier, and all eight authors match the catalog; the reviewed version is arXiv v3. [e01, e03, e06, e10]

problem.text: Full video denoising is expensive, and its action-conditioning value can saturate or deteriorate. The problem is to choose a useful intermediate future representation for each control state, jointly deciding when to terminate and how far to advance if refinement continues.

contributions.text: A paired denoising-depth diagnostic demonstrates substantial state-dependent, non-monotonic action error, motivating intermediate-state selection.
SANTS combines cumulative-hazard stopping with a continuous relative-noise policy, permitting both early termination and nonuniform integration.
Demonstration-based path rewards train only the scheduler, with controlled scheduling and reward ablations testing the resulting computation–quality tradeoff.

inputs: Observation, language, and history conditions supplied to the frozen video–action policy. [e05]
Pooled video-token hidden representation z_k and current noise level σ_k supplied to SANTS. [e03]
Demonstration action chunks used for scheduler post-training rewards. [e06, e16]
outputs: A stopping hazard and a distribution over relative noise-retention ratios. [e04, e05]
A selected intermediate video representation, followed by an action chunk decoded by the frozen action branch. [e03]

steps.name: Expose the current predictive state
steps.detail: A frozen Wan2.2-5B-based video–action Transformer predicts the video flow field. The same forward pass supplies pooled video features to the scheduler, avoiding a separate visual encoder.

steps.name: Choose stopping and progression
steps.detail: A two-layer MLP, with hidden width 512 and bottleneck 256, processes the video feature concatenated with noise level. Separate heads predict a nonnegative hazard increment and the mode and concentration of a Beta-distributed continuation ratio.

steps.name: Update video or hand off to actions
steps.detail: Continuation applies the base sampler's first-order flow update at the selected noise pair. Stopping passes the current representation to the action branch. The stopping decision itself consumes a video forward pass but performs no video-state update.

training.text: For the offline diagnostic, target-domain backbone tuning exposes the action branch to intermediate video noise levels. In the simulation comparison, SANTS uses 30,000 backbone updates followed by 3,000 scheduler updates; external baselines receive the same total adaptation budget. Scheduler training draws on simulated, public real, and self-collected real trajectories.

Each sampled scheduler path is scored after action decoding against a demonstration. Sequence error covers position, quaternion angular distance, and gripper state; temporal-difference error measures motion trends. Motion and gripper events receive extra weight. Two no-gradient reference paths, shallow and fully denoised, normalize quality gains within each input.

Only scheduler parameters change during PPO. Settings include AdamW learning rate 10⁻⁴, weight decay 0.01, four PPO epochs per path, clipping 0.2, gradient norm limit 1.0, EMA baseline decay 0.95, reference regularization weight 0.02, and jump log-probability scale 0.5. There is no entropy bonus or cross-sample reward normalization.

inference.text: Training samples local stop decisions and Beta ratios. Deployment instead stops when cumulative probability F_k exceeds 0.85 and uses the Beta mode deterministically for continuation. Listed noise settings are start 1.00 and forced terminal 0.01; the shallow reference is approximately 0.963.

Action generation remains frozen and separate from physical execution. Policies are queried at action-chunk boundaries. On UR10, each query supplies 16 actions executed at 10 Hz, approximately 1.6 seconds before replanning; no mid-trial teleoperation is allowed.

equations.expression: ΔH_k = softplus(g(z_k, σ_k)); H_k = Σ_{i=1}^k ΔH_i; F_k = 1 − exp(−H_k); h_k = 1 − exp(−ΔH_k).
equations.explanation: H_k accumulates stopping evidence. The conditional probability h_k defines stochastic training decisions, whereas cumulative F_k determines deployment stopping. These probabilities should not be interchanged.
With m_k in (0,1) and c_k > 2, the distribution is unimodal with mode m_k. Smaller ratios retain less noise and make larger progression steps; deployment uses m_k.
The frozen flow predictor updates video latent x_k using the selected noise interval. Here c denotes observation, language, and history conditions, distinct from Beta concentration c_k.

equations.expression: G_m = max(L_m^lo−L_m^hi, ε); u_m = clip((L_m^lo−L_m^τ)/G_m, −1, 1); D_m = max(L_m^lo−L_m^hi,0)/(max(L_m^lo−L_m^hi,0)+κ).
equations.explanation: For sequence and temporal-difference errors, shallow/full anchors define the recoverable gap. Clipping bounds gains, while D_m suppresses positive rewards when full denoising contributes little.

equations.expression: R(τ) = Σ_m w_m[D_m max(u_m,0)−λ_pen max(−u_m,0)] − C(n_τ); with the selected c_1=0, C(n_τ)=0.25 n_τ/N_full.
equations.explanation: Weights are 0.6 for sequence error and 0.4 for temporal differences, with λ_pen=1. The final cost expression is an algebraic simplification of the published schedule under its selected parameters. It penalizes actual video updates, not every forward pass.

results.task: Offline action prediction across video denoising depths
results.setting: 500 manually phase-annotated segments; seven depths from 4% to 100%; fixed initial video/action noise within each segment; masked action MSE normalized to the segment's 4% baseline.
results.metric: Full endpoint not optimal; oracle versus fixed-full normalized MSE
results.value: Reported non-optimal endpoint frequency: coarse 55.65%, fine 41.33%. Oracle means: 0.8433 and 0.6084.
results.interpretation: Intermediate selection has offline action-error headroom. The oracle uses hindsight and ignores computation; these are neither video-fidelity scores nor robot success rates.

results.setting: 50 trials on each of 50 tasks; A100 end-to-end policy latency.
results.value: Reported SANTS: 94.4%, 523.7 ms. Three seed success rates: 94.1%, 94.5%, 94.6%; reported standard deviation 0.3%.
results.interpretation: SANTS has the highest success among these evaluated methods and approximately 81.7% lower latency than LingBot-VA, but Fast-WAM is faster.

results.setting: AgileX and UR10; 50 independent trials per task and method; shared 100-hour adaptation dataset and budget.
results.metric: Unweighted mean task success and average policy latency
results.comparison: Full WAM: 65.7%, 2769.3 ms; π0.5 mean success: 54.6%.
results.interpretation: SANTS improves mean success over full denoising by 7.4 percentage points while reducing latency by 79.0%. It matches or improves every Full WAM task score; fruit sorting remains below π0.5, at 86% versus 92%. These are executed robot trials.

results.setting: RoboTwin 2.0 with fixed backbone, scheduler training budget, and evaluation protocol.
results.comparison: Fixed-5-step: 87.2%, 553.9 ms; Fixed-full: 89.8%, 2769.3 ms; Jump-only: 91.6%, 1137.7 ms; Stop-only: 92.7%, 1329.3 ms.
results.interpretation: The latency-matched fixed schedule loses 7.2 percentage points, supporting state adaptation beyond simple step reduction. Both adaptive decisions contribute under the reported setup.

results.setting: Same frozen backbone, scheduler, training split, budget, and evaluation protocol.
results.comparison: Raw action MSE: 89.7%, 436.3 ms; no difficulty gate: 90.6%, 489.6 ms; no update-cost penalty: 94.9%, 2197.8 ms.
results.interpretation: Normalization and gating improve the observed operating point. Removing computation cost slightly increases success while greatly increasing latency, showing that the full objective explicitly accepts a quality–cost tradeoff.

results.setting: Mean success across seven tasks; target tuning changes only the scheduler.
results.interpretation: Target adaptation helps; the strongest real-robot result includes scheduler tuning.

limitations.text: Evaluation covers one backbone family, RoboTwin 2.0, and two physical platforms. Broader embodiment and camera generalization, joint backbone–scheduler optimization, and adaptation of action-denoising or communication costs remain untested.

If a full anchor is no better than its shallow anchor, D_m becomes zero. That error channel then cannot positively reward even a superior intermediate state. This may hide useful non-monotonic improvements within the phenomenon motivating SANTS.

The update penalty excludes the terminating forward pass and fixed action-decoding work, so it is a proxy for end-to-end latency. Deployment also replaces stochastic training decisions with deterministic rules; the supplied ablations do not isolate that change.

The simulation full-denoising references differ: Table 2 reports LingBot-VA at 92.2% and 2868.4 ms, whereas Table 4 reports Fixed-full at 89.8% and 2769.3 ms. The supplied text does not reconcile their exact configurations. They should not be pooled into one controlled baseline.

Real-robot results lack reported confidence intervals or repeated-training-seed uncertainty. Fifty trials per task support the observed comparisons but do not establish precise uncertainty for small task-level differences.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the intermediate-noise-compatible backbone checkpoint, video-feature extraction interface, nonuniform flow sampler, frozen action decoder, demonstration data, and held-out validation split. Exact source-data composition, split sizes, full-reference update count, and complete feature-pooling and key-frame-weighting implementation are not specified in the supplied text.

Match physical action units and gripper normalization when computing rewards. For UR10, adaptation data are resampled to 15 Hz but inference actions are sent at 10 Hz; reproducing the resulting temporal interpretation requires care. Preserve the documented resets, chunk boundaries, and failure rules.

A focused first experiment would repeat paired depth scans with fixed noise, then compare full SANTS with the latency-matched five-step schedule using identical checkpoints. Record both video updates and forward passes. The paper lists a project page, but no code was inspected and no experiments were reproduced in this reading.

reasoning.text: WAM and efficient inference are supported: future-video features condition actions, and SANTS controls their inference budget. The recorded Dual-system architecture conflicts with the described shared video–action Transformer and its video/action heads. The independent scheduler chooses computation rather than implementing a separate inverse-dynamics policy. Future-conditioned action decoding is compatible with a broad IDM interpretation, but the text does not specify an independent IDM or explicit inverse-dynamics objective. Thus Q4 is not established by this source and warrants editorial review; the recorded snapshot is preserved.

discussionQuestions: Would an additional intermediate anchor recover useful reward signals when full denoising is worse than shallow denoising? [e08, e16]
How much does performance change when deployment samples the trained stopping policy instead of thresholding cumulative hazard? [e04, e12]
Would measured latency rewards, including terminal forward passes and action decoding, change the preferred schedules across hardware? [e05, e17]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author list, project-page line, and arXiv stamp
evidence.detail: The title and eight authors match the catalog. The stamp identifies arXiv:2605.27947v3, dated 26 August 2026; a project URL is listed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1, motivation and scheduling formulation
evidence.detail: The authors distinguish visual refinement from action utility and motivate state-dependent stopping depth and integration spacing.

A frozen video–action Transformer exposes pooled video-token features and a flow prediction. Its action branch conditions on the selected terminal representation; Transformer blocks and both heads remain frozen during scheduler learning.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 3.2, Eqs. (1)–(4) and following paragraph
evidence.detail: Softplus hazard increments accumulate into H_k. Local h_k supplies training probabilities; cumulative F_k is thresholded during deployment.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 3.2, Eqs. (5)–(7) and update-count paragraph
evidence.detail: Continuation samples a Beta noise ratio; mode/concentration parameterization supports deterministic mode deployment. A first-order flow update uses observation, language, and history conditions. Stopping consumes a forward pass without incrementing the update count.
Path rewards compare generated and demonstrated action chunks using sequence and temporal-difference errors, shallow/full normalization, and video-update cost. PPO updates only the scheduler.
Intermediate-noise backbone tuning precedes a frozen-policy scan of 500 manually annotated segments at 4%, 16%, 32%, 48%, 64%, 80%, and 100% depths, holding initial video/action noise fixed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 1 and accompanying oracle discussion
evidence.detail: Full depth is not best for 55.65% of coarse and 41.33% of fine segments. Oracle means are 0.8433/0.6084 versus fixed-full 0.8943/0.6571. The oracle ignores computation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Sections 4.2–4.3, backbone, data, and adaptation setup
evidence.detail: Experiments use a Wan2.2-5B-based policy and multi-source trajectories. Simulation adaptation uses 30,000 backbone plus 3,000 scheduler updates; baseline adaptation uses the same total budget.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 2; p. 7, Section 4.3, simulation results
evidence.detail: SANTS reports 94.4% and 523.7 ms; LingBot-VA 92.2% and 2868.4 ms; Fast-WAM 91.8% and 190 ms. Latency uses A100 GPUs. Evaluation covers 50 trials per 50 tasks; three SANTS seeds give 94.1%, 94.5%, and 94.6%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Table 3 and Section 4.3, real-robot paragraphs
evidence.detail: Mean success is 54.6% for π0.5, 65.7% for Full WAM, and 73.1% for SANTS. Prose confirms Full WAM/SANTS latency of 2769.3/581.3 ms. Fruit sorting is 92%/86%/86%. Each task uses 50 trials.

Fixed-5-step, Fixed-full, Jump-only, Stop-only, and full SANTS respectively report 87.2/89.8/91.6/92.7/94.4% success and 553.9/2769.3/1137.7/1329.3/523.7 ms latency under the stated controlled protocol.
Authors limit generality claims to tested platforms and benchmark, leave joint backbone optimization unexplored, and identify other inference and control costs as future work.

Methods share 100 hours of data, adaptation budget, interfaces, reset distributions, and termination rules. UR10 adaptation uses 15 Hz data; deployment sends 16 predicted actions at 10 Hz before replanning. No mid-trial human correction is allowed.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Appendix B and Tables S1–S2
evidence.detail: The independent scheduler uses two MLP layers, width 512, bottleneck 256, and two heads. Listed settings include start noise 1.00, early reference 0.963, threshold 0.85, and forced terminal 0.01. Transfer/tuned success is 70.6/73.1%, with 0/3000 tuning steps.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 11–12, Appendix C, Action-Quality Error and Eqs. (S1)–(S3); p. 13, Table S3
evidence.detail: Action errors use physical displacement, quaternion angular distance, and normalized gripper BCE, with event weighting. Two-anchor normalization defines bounded gains and a difficulty gate. Quality weights are 0.6/0.4 and negative-gain penalty weight is 1.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix C, Eqs. (S4)–(S5); p. 13, Table S3, cost rows
evidence.detail: Cost is a normalized sum over executed updates. Selected λ_c=0.25, c_0=0.2, and c_1=0 reduce the cost to a linear function of update count.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix C, Path-Level PPO Post-Training and training summary; p. 13, Table S3
evidence.detail: Training samples one policy path and two no-gradient anchors. PPO includes stop and jump likelihoods, an EMA baseline, the stated optimizer/clipping settings, and reference regularization. Validation selects checkpoints using success, path return, and update count.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 12–13, Appendix D and Table S4
evidence.detail: Reward variants hold other settings fixed. Full/raw-MSE/no-gate/no-cost variants report 94.4/89.7/90.6/94.9% success and 523.7/436.3/489.6/2197.8 ms latency. The appendix does not provide additional hyperparameter scans.
